topic: What if you had an iPhone 100 years ago?

script.text: Here's the problem nobody warned you about. Charging. Your charger needs a socket in the wall. Mo's building has electric lights, but no sockets. And lots of homes don't even have lights.
Even in 1940, the census found that more than one in five American homes had no electric lights at all. That's real.

You finally find a socket in a hotel lobby. You plug in. Nothing. Parts of New York still run on direct current, the old kind of electricity. Your charger was built for the other kind. You lose a whole day, and twelve percent, hunting for the right socket.
In the end you pay a hotel porter a whole dollar to let you sit behind the front desk, next to the only socket that works, while the guests stare at the glowing brick on the counter.
Then there's the bigger problem. Look at what you're holding. The chip inside a recent iPhone can do thirty-five trillion operations every second.

The most famous computer of the next twenty years, ENIAC, won't be switched on until 1946. It will weigh twenty-seven tonnes, fill a whole room, burn a hundred and fifty kilowatts of power, and do five thousand additions a second. That's real too.
You're carrying a machine the world won't be able to build for half a century. And you've been showing it off in jazz clubs.
The newspapers stop calling it a lightning box. Now they just call it the device.

script.beat: fact: the price of a call
script.text: In January 1927, people will pay seventy-five dollars to talk to London for three minutes. That's well over a thousand dollars in today's money. That's real. So imagine what someone would pay for the thing in your pocket.

science.claim: Even in 1940, more than one in five American homes had no electric lights.
science.working: The 1940 Census found 78.7% of all occupied housing units had electric lights, so 21.3% did not: more than one in five.
science.source: US Census Bureau, History and the Census: Electricity

science.claim: Parts of New York still ran on direct current in the 1920s.
science.working: Edison's DC distribution served much of Manhattan into the 20th century; Con Edison only ended its last DC service in 2007.
science.source: Con Edison / New York Times, 'Con Ed Shuts Down Last of Its DC Service' (Nov 2007)

science.claim: The chip inside a recent iPhone can do 35 trillion operations every second.
science.working: The A17 Pro (iPhone 15 Pro) has a 16-core Neural Engine rated at 35 trillion operations per second.
science.source: Apple, A17 Pro announcement (Sept 2023); Wikipedia: Apple A17 Pro

science.claim: ENIAC, switched on in 1946, weighed 27 tonnes, used 150 kW and did 5,000 additions a second.
science.working: ENIAC was announced 14 February 1946; it weighed more than 30 short tons (27 t), consumed 150 kW, and performed 5,000 additions or subtractions per second.

science.claim: In January 1927, a three-minute call to London cost $75; well over $1,000 today.
science.working: Commercial New York-London telephone service opened 7 January 1927 at $75 for the first three minutes. CPI-U 1927 = 17.4, 2024 = 313.7: 75 x 313.7 / 17.4 = about $1,350.
science.source: This Day in Tech History (First Transatlantic Telephone Call); BLS CPI-U annual averages
